item.research_question: What is the origin of the superior strength and plasticity in the CrCoNi alloy compared to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, and how do magnetic properties influence the phase stability between fcc and hcp structures?
item.material_system: CrCoNi (ternary), CrMnFeCoNi (quinary), FeCoNi, MnCoNi, MnFeNi (equiatomic ternary derivatives)
item.processing_route: Alloys prepared as single-phase fcc solid solutions; samples deformed to approximately 55% true strain; DFT calculations using VASP with GGA-PBE, quasi-harmonic approximation for vibrational entropy, and special quasi-random structures (SQS); atomistic simulations using classical potentials on fcc Co as a surrogate.
item.test_conditions: Cryogenic to room temperature regimes relevant to experiments; shear deformations inducing stacking faults and twin interfaces; magnetic and non-magnetic DFT calculations; atomic resolution STEM in HAADF mode along 110 and 101 zone axes.
key_findings: CrCoNi exhibits a distinctly lower-energy hcp phase compared to fcc at low temperatures, driven by vibrational entropy, whereas CrMnFeCoNi shows negligible energy difference due to magnetic frustration.

In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is favored over fcc even when magnetic effects are turned off, while in Mn-containing alloys (MnCoNi, MnFeNi), magnetism reduces the energy difference between phases to nearly zero.

Mn atoms exhibit magnetic frustration with moments fluctuating between approximately 3 and -3 μB regardless of environment, unlike Cr moments which show a narrower distribution and stronger dependence on local chemistry.

The average stacking fault energy in CrCoNi is negative, indicating a driving force for fcc-to-hcp transformation, whereas in CrMnFeCoNi, energy overlaps between stable and unstable structures prevent a clear driving force.
Hcp laths in CrCoNi form localized to stacking faults and twin interfaces via the glide of 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations, rather than as a bulk transformation.
Dislocation interactions with twin boundaries in CrCoNi lead to the nucleation of 3-layer hcp structures, which act as barriers to slip while redirecting shear to prevent stress concentration.
The hcp phase in CrCoNi can heal back to fcc upon removal of stress or interaction with intersecting slip systems, allowing for recovery without loss of plasticity.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the superior mechanical properties of CrCoNi arise from a magnetically-driven fcc-to-hcp phase transformation triggered by dislocation slip. In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is intrinsically lower in energy (ground state) at low temperatures, and the absence of magnetic frustration allows this transformation to proceed readily at stacking faults and twin boundaries. This creates nanostructured hcp laths that strengthen the material by blocking dislocations while simultaneously redirecting shear to avoid crack initiation. In contrast, the addition of Mn in CrMnFeCoNi introduces magnetic frustration, which eliminates the energy difference between fcc and hcp phases, suppressing the transformation and resulting in inferior mechanical performance.
item.limitations: Free energy calculations for the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy pose significant practical challenges and yielded non-conclusive estimates; the study uses fcc Co as a surrogate system for atomistic simulations of dislocation interactions in CrCoNi due to the lack of reliable interatomic potentials for the Ni-Co-Cr system.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that new alloying combinations can be predicted based on favorable magnetic properties to design single-phase alloys with metastable structures, emphasizing that high-entropy alloys with more constituent elements are not necessarily superior to their derivatives.
quotes: This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy.
In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is consistently favored over fcc, even when the magnetic effects are turned off.
Mn moment switches between positive and negative values in both phases, and Fe appears to experience negative magnetic moments in the hcp structure.
